title: Getting around, and the word for "not"
goal: Get around the city by metro, microbus, and taxi — while mastering the only way to negate a verb in Egyptian: the مـ...ـش wrapper.
bekal: negate verbs with the مـ...ـش wrapper in every form
take the metro, microbuses, and taxis without paying the wrong fare
tell when to use مش and when to use the wrapper

dialogs.title: حوار — في التاكسي
dialogs.intro: It's evening, and Budi flags down a white taxi in Dokki to go home to Ma'adi.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: Ma'adi, please. Is the meter on?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: Thanks. Is the traffic bad today?

lines.speaker: السواق:
lines.text: مش أوي. بس ماتاخدش الكورنيش، فيه حادثة.
lines.baca: mish ’awi. bas matakhudsh il-kurniish, fiih hadsa.
lines.id: Not too bad. But don't take the Corniche — there's been an accident.
lines.literal: not very. but don't-you-take the-Corniche, there-is accident.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: أنا مابعرفش الطرق كويس. انت أدرى.
lines.baca: ana maba‘rafsh iṭ-ṭuru’ kuwayyis. inta adra.
lines.id: I don't know the roads well. You know best.
lines.literal: I not-I-know the-roads well. you more-knowing.

lines.speaker: السواق:
lines.text: انت مش مصري صح؟ بتتكلم عربي حلو.
lines.baca: inta mish maṣri ṣahh? bititkallim ‘arabi hilw.
lines.id: You're not Egyptian, right? You speak good Arabic.
lines.literal: you not Egyptian right? you-speak Arabic sweet.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: من إندونيسيا. بس لسه مابفهمش كل حاجة.
lines.baca: min Indunisya. bas lissa mabafhamsh kull haaga.
lines.id: I'm from Indonesia. But I still don't understand everything.
lines.literal: from Indonesia. but still not-I-understand every thing.

lines.speaker: السواق:
lines.text: معلش، الأول صعب. انت بتركب المترو؟
lines.baca: ma‘lesh, il-awwil ṣa‘b. inta bitirkab il-mitro?
lines.id: Don't worry, the beginning is hard. Do you take the metro?
lines.literal: never-mind, the-first difficult. you you-ride the-metro?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: أيوه، كل يوم. بس بالليل مابركبش.
lines.baca: aywa, kull yōm. bas bil-lēl mabarkabsh.
lines.id: Yes, every day. But not at night.
lines.literal: yes, every day. but at-the-night not-I-ride.

lines.speaker: السواق:
lines.text: صح. بالليل التاكسي أحسن. أهو وصلنا.
lines.baca: ṣahh. bil-lēl it-taksi ahsan. ahu waṣalna.
lines.id: Right. At night a taxi's better. Here we are.
lines.literal: right. at-the-night the-taxi better. there-it-is we-arrived.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: Here's seventy. I don't have any change.

lines.speaker: السواق:
lines.text: ولا يهمك. ربنا يخليك، تصبح على خير.
lines.baca: wala yihimmak. rabbina yikhalliik, tiṣbah ‘ala khēr.
lines.id: No problem. God bless you, good night.
lines.literal: not it-concerns-you. our-Lord keeps-you, may-you-wake on good.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: وانت من أهل الخير. تصبح على خير.
lines.baca: w inta min ahl il-khēr. tiṣbah ‘ala khēr.
lines.literal: and you from people the-good. may-you-wake on good.

notes: **The wrapper مـ...ـش hugs the whole verb from both sides.** The prefix مـ goes in front, the ending ـش at the back, and the verb keeps its بـ. So بعرف becomes مابعرفش, and بفهم becomes مابفهمش. This wrapper also exists in Moroccan, Tunisian, and Palestinian Arabic — but not in Fusha at all.

**The ending ـش is what's left of the word شيء, "thing".** Originally the sentence was "I don't know a thing", much like French with *ne* and *pas*. Over time the second part stuck on as an ending, and now it can't be removed.
**For future verbs with حـ, use مش, not the wrapper.** مش حاروح (I won't go), not ماحاروحش. This is the only verb negated with مش, and the reason will become clearer in unit 13.

**The word أهو means "here it is, there it is", pointing to something that's just appeared.** The feminine is أهي, the plural أهم. It's one of the most typically Egyptian words and has no direct equivalent in Fusha or in English.

**The phrase مامعييش فكة means "I don't have any change on me".** Notice that معايا ("with me", meaning "I have on me") is treated like a verb: it's negated with the wrapper, not with مش. The same goes for عندي and فيه.
**The real way to say good night is تصبح على خير**, literally "may you wake up to goodness". The reply is وانت من أهل الخير. This pair is one of the loveliest in everyday Egyptian.

grammars.title: The مـ...ـش wrapper in every form
body: There's one rule and it works for every person: put مـ in front of the whole verb including its prefix, and ـش after the whole thing including its ending.
after: Look at the three rows with endings: ـي on انتي and ـوا on انتوا and هما **lengthen** when ـش is added — بتفهمي becomes مابتفهميش. That long vowel is what keeps the ـش audible.
The same wrapper is used for past-tense verbs: ماشربتش (I didn't drink), ماراحش (he didn't go), ماكلناش (we didn't eat). No extra rules at all.
The same wrapper is also used for telling someone not to do something: ماتشربش (don't drink), ماتروحش (don't go), ماتنساش (don't forget). The prohibition uses the انت form without بـ.

grammars.title: The word مش or the wrapper — a decision table
body: This is the table to look at again whenever you're unsure. The rule fits in one sentence: if the sentence has a verb marked with بـ or in the past tense, use the wrapper; otherwise use مش.
after: The three middle rows — عند، مع، فيه — are the ones people get wrong most often. All three are prepositions, not verbs, but because they stand in for a verb, Egyptian treats them like one.

If you slip and use مش with a بـ verb, people will still understand — and it's sometimes used on purpose for emphasis: أنا مش بشتغل هنا sounds like "it's not that I work here". But as the standard form, use the wrapper.

blocks.text: The Cairo metro has one thing you need to know from day one: the two middle cars of every train are reserved for women — عربية السيدات *‘arabeyyit is-sayyidaat*. Men who get on there will be asked to move, while women can ride in any car.

blocks.title: Taking a microbus without panicking
items: Microbuses have no fixed stops. You flag one down with a hand signal, and to get off you call out على جنب لو سمحت *‘ala ganb law samaht* (pull over, please).
You pay by passing your money forward through the passengers in front of you to the driver, and your change comes back the same way. The system runs entirely on trust and almost never fails.
To ask whether a microbus is going your way: رايح المعادي؟ Any answer that isn't a nod usually means no.

sections.title: The negative sentences you'll need most

blocks.text: Most of the sentences that rescue a foreigner are negative ones. These are worth memorizing whole.

head: مصري
Say it
Meaning
rows: no thanks, I don't want any

blocks.text: The phrase مش عايز، شكراً is worth practicing until it comes out without thinking. At Cairo's tourist sites you'll be offered goods, services, and rides dozens of times a day, and answering calmly in Egyptian works far better than silence or answering in English.

exercises.prompt: Fill in مش or the right wrapped form.

items: I don't understand — say it again slowly.
I don't have any change on me.
Don't take the Corniche, there's been an accident.
I don't take the metro at night.
